rationale:
Evidence: iteration 5 is the best design so far (356.57). Its oval track finished in 17 of 20 trials (mean 1.88 s), so the robot can complete the course within the 3 s limit at speed 0.9. The s-bend (progress 0.38) and slalom (progress 0.12) still end off track, with max_error about 0.063 to 0.065 m just past the 0.06 m floor and one line-loss event per run. Steering oscillation (0.16 to 0.28) is moderate, so the failure is lateral excursion on the bends rather than jitter. The off-track limit is max(0.06, 0.0125 + body_width/4), which stays at 0.06 for every allowed body width, so geometry cannot widen it.

The move from y = 0.05 to y = 0.07 m, together with the speed drop, gave the largest gain across iterations. The sensor row is now close to the forward limit of 0.08 m. Iteration 5 changed both the sensor row and the speed, so I cannot separate their effects. I keep the speed and controller gains fixed and move only the sensor row forward to y = 0.08 m. This tests whether more lead on the bends further reduces the s-bend and slalom excursions while the oval still finishes.

Changes: (1) sensor row moved from y = 0.07 to 0.08 m, the top of the allowed range, for earlier sight of the line. (2) Everything else is unchanged from iteration 5: five sensors at x = -0.04 to +0.04 m in 0.02 m steps, 16 mm footprint, wheel track 0.12 m, wheel radius 0.03 m, body 0.16 x 0.12 m, mass 0.6 kg, base_speed 0.9, kp 2.0, ki 0, kd 1.0, weights [-2,-1,0,1,2], last_direction line loss.

Expected result: oval completion stays near 85 percent, and s-bend and slalom progress rises from 0.38 and 0.12 toward roughly 0.45 and 0.2. The score should improve modestly, to about 370 to 420. The main risk is that the extra lead adds phase error and raises rms_error or oscillation, which the revision rounds should check.
